name: Wide / establishing shot
purpose: Orients the viewer in the space before anything happens; shows full body plus surroundings so a viewer can copy a movement or judge scale.
when_to_use: Opening shot of a tutorial or demo; any moment you need the audience to see the whole setup (e.g. a home-workout routine in a small room).
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy (Michael Wiese Productions, 2009)

name: Medium shot
purpose: Balances context and facial expression; the default 'talking and doing' shot.
when_to_use: Main narration/demo shots where you need to see both the presenter's face and their hands/body doing something.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Close-up
purpose: Heightens emotional intensity or draws attention to a specific detail (face, product, hands).
when_to_use: Emotional beats, product reveals, or 'watch exactly how I do this' form-check moments.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Extreme close-up
purpose: Isolates one detail to create tension, curiosity, or precision (an eye, an ingredient, a number on a screen).
when_to_use: Hook moments in the first 3 seconds, or a single critical detail (a mistake, a result number).
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Point-of-view (POV) shot
purpose: Puts the viewer directly in the subject's perspective, increasing immersion and empathy.
when_to_use: Showing 'what you'll see when you do this' in a tutorial, or building suspense in a story-driven video.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Over-the-shoulder shot
purpose: Frames a conversation or demonstration from behind one participant, keeping both people connected in-frame.
when_to_use: Interviews, two-person dialogue, or a 'watching someone do something' teaching moment.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Low angle
purpose: Camera looks up at the subject, making them appear powerful, confident, or dominant.
when_to_use: Authority-building moments (a coach demonstrating expertise, a confident brand statement).
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: High angle
purpose: Camera looks down at the subject, making them appear smaller, vulnerable, or relatable.
when_to_use: Showing struggle, vulnerability, or a 'before' state in a transformation story.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Dutch / tilted angle
purpose: Tilts the horizon to create unease, disorientation, or energy.
when_to_use: Comedic beats, chaotic moments, or 'something's off' storytelling cues. Use sparingly — overuse reads as amateurish.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Dolly-in / push-in
purpose: Camera moves slowly toward the subject, building emotional intensity and drawing the viewer into a moment.
when_to_use: Reveal moments, emotional peaks, or the climax of a mistake/lesson story.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Dolly-out / pull-out
purpose: Camera moves away from the subject, revealing context or creating a sense of resolution.
when_to_use: Ending shots, revealing the full result of a transformation, or comedic context-reveals.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Tracking / follow shot
purpose: Camera moves alongside the subject, maintaining energy and continuity of action.
when_to_use: Walk-and-talk intros, action B-roll, or following a process from start to finish.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Handheld
purpose: Slight camera instability reads as authentic, urgent, or 'in the moment' — the opposite of polished.
when_to_use: Vlogging, behind-the-scenes segments, or moments meant to feel raw/unscripted.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Static / locked-off shot
purpose: A perfectly still frame lets the action or performance carry the shot without camera distraction.
when_to_use: Tutorial demonstration shots where the viewer needs to study the movement without camera noise.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Whip pan
purpose: A fast, blurred camera swing that creates an energetic or comedic transition between two shots.
when_to_use: Fast-paced cuts between scenes, comedic beats, or high-energy Shorts/Reels editing.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Cutaway / insert shot
purpose: A brief shot of a supporting detail (hands, an object, a phone screen) that adds information without breaking the main shot's continuity.
when_to_use: Showing an ingredient, a product feature, or a step's result while the main narration continues.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Reaction shot
purpose: Shows a person's emotional response to something just seen or said, building empathy and pacing.
when_to_use: Testimonial moments, comedic timing, or letting a 'wow' reaction sell a result.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Two-shot
purpose: Frames two people together in one shot, visually establishing their relationship or dynamic.
when_to_use: Collaboration content, interviews, or family/relationship-driven storytelling.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

definition: People feel obligated to return a favor or value they've received.
hook_application: Give the viewer something useful (a tip, a laugh, a free resource) before asking for a follow, like, or purchase — the 'jab before the right hook' idea.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini (HarperBusiness); Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: People assign more value to things that are limited in availability or time.
hook_application: Time-boxed or limited-availability framing in a hook or CTA ('only works for the next 24 hours', 'limited spots').
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: People are more easily persuaded by sources they perceive as credible or expert.
hook_application: Open with a credential, a data point, or a demonstrated result before giving advice — signals the video is worth trusting.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: People look to others' behavior to decide what's correct, especially under uncertainty.
hook_application: Framing like '1 million people already tried this' or showing real comments/results builds trust fast in a hook.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: People are more easily persuaded by people they like or feel similar to.
hook_application: Relatable framing, shared identity/language (local slang, regional dialect), humor, and authenticity increase a hook's pull.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: Once people commit to something small, they feel pressure to act consistently with that commitment.
hook_application: Small early CTAs ('comment DAY 1', 'save this for later') build toward larger asks (subscribe, buy) later in a series.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: Shared group identity ('people like us') deepens persuasion beyond simple liking.
hook_application: Framing content around a shared identity ('for Mumbai flat-dwellers', 'for working moms') increases relevance and trust.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini (added in later editions)

steps: Character (the audience is the hero)
Problem (external, internal, philosophical)
Guide (the brand, positioned as mentor not hero)
Plan (a clear, simple path forward)
Call to action
Success (what happens if they follow the plan)
Failure (what happens if they don't)
video_application: Frame the creator/brand as the guide and the viewer as the hero with a problem; the video becomes the 'plan', the CTA is explicit, and showing both the payoff and the cost of inaction increases follow-through.

steps: State the problem the audience has
Agitate it — make the pain concrete and immediate
Solve it with your content/product
video_application: Classic short-form hook structure: name the pain point in the first line, twist the knife briefly, then deliver the fix — works especially well for 'mistake' and 'myth-busting' video formats.

steps: Show the 'before' state (the struggle)
Show the 'after' state (the transformation/result)
Show the 'bridge' — how to get from one to the other
video_application: Ideal for transformation content (fitness, skincare, home organization) — open on the after/result to hook curiosity, then walk back to show the bridge.

steps: Setup (introduce character/situation)
Confrontation (the obstacle or complication)
Resolution (the outcome)
video_application: Even a 60-second video benefits from a compressed 3-act shape: a few seconds of setup, the bulk of the video on the obstacle/attempt, and a clear payoff at the end.

steps: Monitor breaking news/trends in your niche
Move fast — the window is hours, not days
Attach your brand/expertise to the trend with a genuine angle, not a forced tie-in
video_application: React to a trending topic in your niche (a viral claim, a new product, a seasonal event) within the trend's live window to capture algorithmic reach that evergreen content can't get on its own.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott (Wiley)

steps: Define the specific audience segment (not 'everyone')
Identify their language, pain points, and platform habits
Tailor the story's problem/solution to that exact segment
video_application: The niche-specificity principle from your earlier research (e.g. 'home workouts for Mumbai flats' vs generic 'fitness') is a direct application of buyer-persona thinking to video content.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott

steps: Publish directly to your audience instead of relying on gatekeepers (press, algorithms alone)
Build owned channels (email list, community) alongside platform reach
Use consistency and authenticity over polish
video_application: Encourages creators to treat YouTube/Instagram as a direct relationship channel — consistent posting and community reply builds compounding trust beyond any single video's performance.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott

steps: Exposition (setup)
Rising action (building complication)
Climax (peak tension/turning point)
Falling action (consequences unfold)
Resolution (final outcome)
video_application: A more granular alternative to the 3-act structure for longer-form videos (5-10+ min) — gives two extra beats (rising/falling action) to build and release tension around a demonstration or story.
further_reading: Academic narrative theory; referenced in Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (Monique Schröder, Copenhagen Business School, 2015)

steps: Hero — the one with the goal (your viewer)
Mentor/Guide — the one who helps (your brand/creator)
Threshold/obstacle — what stands in the way
video_application: Mirrors StoryBrand's Character+Guide structure; useful when scripting a video as a mini-journey rather than a flat list of tips — gives the viewer a role to see themselves in.
further_reading: Joseph Campbell's monomyth; referenced in Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (Monique Schröder, 2015)

steps: Draw the viewer into a story world (vivid, specific detail)
Reduce their critical/skeptical distance while 'inside' the story
Deliver the message/CTA while transportation is highest
video_application: Explains why a specific, concrete anecdote ('I tried this for 30 days and...') out-persuades a generic claim — specificity increases immersion, which increases persuasion.
further_reading: Narrative transportation theory (Green & Brock); referenced in Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (Monique Schröder, 2015)

template: [Action], ghar pe/apne shehar mein, bina [barrier], sirf [duration] minute — chalo shuru
[Pain point] ka time ya resource nahi hai?
Ye [number] galtiyan tumhara [outcome] kharab kar rahi hain
[Common belief] band karo. Iske bajaye [alternative] karo.
[Number] logo ne yeh try kiya — result dekho
[Number]% log yeh galat karte hain — sahi tareeka yeh hai

definition: Instead of chasing only mass-market topics, highly specific niche content can profitably reach a small, exact audience directly online — the audience doesn't need to be huge to be valuable.
video_application: Directly validates the micro-niche-specificity finding from earlier research: a video for 'budget skincare for Indian women in tier-2 cities' reaches a smaller but far more responsive audience than a generic 'skincare tips' video.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 2

definition: Publishing genuine expertise directly to your audience (rather than through media gatekeepers) builds long-term trust and authority.
video_application: A creator who consistently teaches real, useful expertise builds compounding channel trust that outlasts any single viral hit — supports prioritizing a content pillar/series strategy over one-off videos.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 3

definition: Actively tracking what's said about you across social platforms and blogs surfaces both opportunities (trending questions) and problems (complaints) early.
video_application: Creators should monitor their own comments and niche conversations to catch a recurring question or complaint that can become the next video topic — a low-cost, high-relevance content-idea source.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 5

definition: Content spreads virally when several independent communities each find their own reason to share it around the same time, rather than from one single push or channel.
video_application: Design a video to give multiple distinct audiences (e.g. fitness beginners AND busy parents AND budget-conscious viewers) their own reason to share it, instead of targeting only one angle.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 8

definition: The depth and usefulness of an entire content ecosystem — not any single polished asset — drives discoverability and credibility.
video_application: Supports the series/playlist strategy over isolated videos: a channel with a deep, organized back-catalog on a niche out-performs one with scattered unrelated uploads, both for search and for viewer trust.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 9

definition: The same core story or message is adapted across multiple formats (blog, audio, video, forum discussion) to meet different audiences where their consumption habits already are.
video_application: Repurpose one core hook/story across YouTube long-form, Shorts, and community posts so the same message reinforces itself across touchpoints instead of existing only once.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 4-6

definition: Every brand or creator has an underlying 'why' — the founding reason and values behind what they do — and this core story should ground every piece of content, even when only a simplified version is shown externally.
video_application: Before scripting individual videos, define your channel's one-sentence 'why' (e.g. 'I make fitness accessible for people with no time or equipment'). Every video's hook and CTA should trace back to that core story so the channel feels coherent over time, not like disconnected one-offs.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder (Copenhagen Business School, 2015), citing Fog et al. 2010

definition: Organizations (and by extension creators) tell a simple, external-facing story day-to-day, while a more complex internal story explains the full context of decisions and direction.
video_application: The short hook/caption is your 'operational' story (simple, external); your channel's about section or a longer-form video can carry the fuller 'strategic' story of why you make this content — keep both consistent with each other.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, citing Madsen-Mygdal 2014

definition: Storytelling in an organization serves four distinct functions: internal leadership (aligning a team around shared values), marketing communication (engaging an audience emotionally), external stakeholder narratives (how others talk about you, which you don't fully control), and cultural sensemaking (helping people understand their own identity through the story).
video_application: A creator's storytelling operates in at least two of these lanes: marketing communication (the video itself) and cultural sensemaking (why the audience relates to and shares it) — a video that only sells but doesn't help the audience make sense of their own situation misses the sensemaking function that drives sharing.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, Ch. 3.3.1

definition: A brand or piece of content becomes more meaningful to someone the more closely it connects to their own sense of identity — people process content partly to satisfy their own psychological need to make sense of their world.
video_application: Content that helps a viewer understand their own situation (e.g. 'why you're always tired even after 8 hours of sleep') creates a deeper connection than content that only demonstrates a product or skill, because it ties into the viewer's self-understanding.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, citing Escalas 2004

principle: Story building blocks (audience, message, conflict, character, plot, action)
definition: Across the literature, the recurring elements needed for an effective story are: a clearly understood target audience, a clear message, a conflict/challenge, relatable characters, a plot, and a resulting action.
video_application: A practical pre-shoot checklist: name your audience specifically, state your one message in a sentence, name the conflict/pain point, decide who the 'character' is (usually the viewer or the creator), sketch the plot beats, and confirm the action you want the viewer to take.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, Ch. 5.2.3

principle: Repetition as the true success signal
definition: Genuine storytelling success isn't just the audience showing interest once — it's when they repeat or retell the story themselves, which signals real engagement and impact.
video_application: Track not just views/likes but whether viewers repeat your framing in comments, duets, or their own captions — that's a stronger signal of a hook or story actually landing than raw view count alone.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, Ch. 5.2.4, citing Mills 2008

concept: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook framework
definition: A boxing metaphor for content cadence: 'jabs' are lightweight, generous content that entertains/engages without asking for anything (builds the relationship), while the 'right hook' is the direct call to action/sales ask. Most content should be jabs; the right hook only lands well after enough jabs have built trust.
video_application: Plan a content calendar where most videos give pure value with no ask (comedy, tips, entertainment) and only occasionally does a video carry a direct CTA — matches the earlier commitment/consistency and reciprocity persuasion principles already in this dataset.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk (HarperBusiness, 2013)

definition: Content is tailored to the specific culture, format, and language norms of the platform it's posted on, rather than reposting the same asset everywhere.
video_application: A hook that works as on-screen text on a Reel may need a completely different pacing/format as a YouTube Short or a long-form intro — don't just resize the same video across platforms.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Effective content blends into the viewer's normal browsing/entertainment experience and feels like part of the conversation, not an ad breaking into it.
video_application: Open videos the way the platform's native creators talk to their audience, not the way a traditional TV ad opens — avoid a 'commercial' tone in the first few seconds.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Most content should be generous — giving value, entertainment, or community connection — without an ask attached; overwhelming the audience with sales pitches erodes trust.
video_application: Reserve explicit CTAs for a minority of videos; let most videos simply deliver on the hook's promise without pivoting to a sales ask.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Content that connects to current trends or shared cultural moments feels timely and relatable, increasing engagement.
video_application: Pairs with the earlier 'newsjacking' concept — tie a niche topic to something currently trending in the broader culture when there's a genuine, non-forced connection.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Small, timely, culturally-relevant snippets keep a brand or creator agile and able to react quickly, rather than relying only on big, infrequent productions.
video_application: Favor a steady stream of short, timely videos/Shorts alongside occasional bigger productions — agility beats a slow, over-produced release schedule.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Content reinforces a recognizable identity across platforms and stays aware of the brand's/creator's own tone and limits, rather than chasing every trend regardless of fit.
video_application: Ties to the earlier core-story principle — every video, hook, and CTA should feel recognizably 'you' even as formats vary by platform.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

note: Visual-first, closed-loop-sharing platforms are well-suited to establishing brand story and identity ('jabs') but make a direct call-to-action harder to execute smoothly — CTAs need to feel native (e.g. 'link in bio', a caption prompt) rather than an overt sales push in the visual itself.
video_application: On Reels/Instagram, put more weight on visual storytelling and identity-building; move harder CTAs to captions, bio links, or a dedicated occasional post rather than forcing them into every visual.
source: general_marketing_knowledge (platform specifics like exact algorithms have changed since 2013; verify current mechanics separately)
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk, Ch. 6

jab_hook_balance: engagement unlocks reach for the hook
note: On algorithmic feed platforms, engagement on 'jab' content increases the algorithm's willingness to show later 'right hook' content — engagement is a prerequisite, not a side effect.
video_application: Build engagement habits (comments, shares) with value-first content before posting a conversion-focused video, so the platform's distribution system already favors your channel.
source: general_marketing_knowledge (specific algorithm names like EdgeRank are outdated; the underlying principle — engagement gates reach — still generally applies)
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk, Ch. 3
